2025_131_2025_masb_board_of_director_sla.paragraph: Michigan Association of School Boards election materials distributed to the Troy School District Board of Education for its February 25, 2025 meeting present the 2025 slate of candidates for the MASB Board of Directors, along with the Article IV membership bylaws that divide active members into eight ISD-based regions and seven pupil-membership groups. The largest contest on the ballot is Region 8 (Macomb ISD, Oakland Schools and Wayne RESA) for a three-year term, and the packet reproduces the full election statements of its candidates; Region 6 has a one-year term and Region 7 a three-year term.
2025_131_2025_masb_board_of_director_sla.page:
**What it is**
The 2025 Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB) Board of Directors candidate slate, packaged with MASB Bylaws Article IV (Membership) and the association's board-election and email-voting procedures. Included in the Troy School District Board of Education agenda for February 25, 2025. Incumbents are shown in bold in the original.

**Structure of MASB membership (Bylaws Article IV, Section 2)**
The board of education of any public school district in Michigan may become an active member. Active members are divided into eight regions designated by intermediate school district boundaries:
- Region 1: Copper Country ISD, Delta-Schoolcraft ISD, Dickinson-Iron ISD, Eastern Upper Peninsula ISD, Gogebic-Ontonagon ISD, Marquette-Alger RESA, Menominee County ISD
- Region 2: Alpena-Montmorency-Alcona ESD, Charlevoix-Emmet ISD, Cheboygan-Otsego-Presque Isle ESD, COOR ISD, Iosco RESA, Manistee ISD, Northwest Education Services, Wexford-Missaukee ISD
- Region 3: Ionia County ISD, Kent ISD, Mecosta-Osceola ISD, Montcalm Area ISD, Muskegon Area ISD, Newaygo County RESA, Ottawa Area ISD, West Shore ESD
- Region 4: Bay-Arenac ISD, Clare-Gladwin RESD, Clinton County RESA, Gratiot-Isabella RESD, Midland County ESA, Saginaw ISD, Shiawassee RESD
- Region 5: Genesee ISD, Huron ISD, Lapeer County ISD, Sanilac ISD, St. Clair County RESA, Tuscola ISD
- Region 6: Allegan Area ESA, Barry ISD, Berrien RESA, Branch ISD, Calhoun ISD, Heritage Southwest ISD, Kalamazoo RESA, St. Joseph County ISD, Van Buren ISD
- Region 7: Eaton RESA, Hillsdale County ISD, Ingham ISD, Jackson County ISD, Lenawee ISD, Livingston ESA, Monroe County ISD, Washtenaw ISD
- Region 8: Macomb ISD, Oakland Schools, Wayne RESA

Members are also divided into seven groups by pupil membership: Group I, all intermediate districts; Group II, 0-1,400; Group III, 1,401-2,500; Group IV, 2,501-5,000; Group V, 5,001-11,000; Group VI, 11,001-40,000; Group VII, more than 40,000.

Contests identified are Region 6 (One-Year Term), Region 7 (Three-Year Term) and Region 8 (Three-Year Term).

**Region 8 candidates and credentials**
The excerpt reproduces full election statements for the Region 8 three-year-term field: Dr. Anisha Hannah (Pontiac), Jason Babbage (Allen Park), Roderick Means (Westwood Community), Paul Kolin (Bloomfield Hills), Randel Meisner (Fitzgerald), Scott Wallace (Fraser), Lisa Valerio-Nowc (Clintondale) and Ursula (Wester) Rogers (Romulus). Reported board tenures range from 2 years to 28 years, and MASB certification levels range from Certified Boardmember Award and Award of Merit up through Award of Distinction, Master Boardmember, Master Diamond, Master Platinum and the President's Award.

**Recurring themes in the statements**
Sustainable and equitable funding for public education, full funding for special education, offsetting MPSERS cost, teacher retention and shortages, declining enrollment, student mental health, educational technology, and advocacy in Lansing.
2025_131_2025_masb_board_of_director_sla.verbose:
**Document and context.** MASB 2025 election materials placed before the Troy School District Board of Education for its meeting of February 25, 2025. The packet combines the Michigan Association of School Boards Bylaws, Article IV (Membership), the table of contents entry for "Board of Directors' Elections - Candidate Information and Email Voting Procedures" (page 4), and the candidate statements headed "2025 ELECTIONS - CANDIDATES FOR MASB BOARD of DIRECTORS." A note states that incumbents are bolded in the original.

**Bylaws, Article IV, Section 2 - Active Members.** The board of education of any public school district in Michigan may become an active member of the association. Active members are divided into eight regions designated according to intermediate school district boundaries. Region 1 comprises Copper Country ISD, Delta-Schoolcraft ISD, Dickinson-Iron ISD, Eastern Upper Peninsula ISD, Gogebic-Ontonagon ISD, Marquette-Alger RESA and Menominee County ISD. Region 2 comprises Alpena-Montmorency-Alcona ESD, Charlevoix-Emmet ISD, Cheboygan-Otsego-Presque Isle ESD, COOR ISD, Iosco RESA, Manistee ISD, Northwest Education Services and Wexford-Missaukee ISD. Region 3 comprises Ionia County ISD, Kent ISD, Mecosta-Osceola ISD, Montcalm Area ISD, Muskegon Area ISD, Newaygo County RESA, Ottawa Area ISD and West Shore ESD. Region 4 comprises Bay-Arenac ISD, Clare-Gladwin RESD, Clinton County RESA, Gratiot-Isabella RESD, Midland County ESA, Saginaw ISD and Shiawassee RESD. Region 5 comprises Genesee ISD, Huron ISD, Lapeer County ISD, Sanilac ISD, St. Clair County RESA and Tuscola ISD. Region 6 comprises Allegan Area ESA, Barry ISD, Berrien RESA, Branch ISD, Calhoun ISD, Heritage Southwest ISD, Kalamazoo RESA, St. Joseph County ISD and Van Buren ISD. Region 7 comprises Eaton RESA, Hillsdale County ISD, Ingham ISD, Jackson County ISD, Lenawee ISD, Livingston ESA, Monroe County ISD and Washtenaw ISD. Region 8 comprises Macomb ISD, Oakland Schools and Wayne RESA - the region in which Troy School District, an Oakland Schools constituent, votes. Active members are also divided into seven groups based on pupil membership: Group I, all intermediate districts; Group II, districts with pupil membership of 0-1,400; Group III, 1,401-2,500; Group IV, 2,501-5,000; Group V, 5,001-11,000; Group VI, 11,001-40,000; and Group VII, more than 40,000.

**Candidate slate.** Candidates are listed with their districts, counties and packet page numbers: TiAnna Harrison, Kalamazoo Public Schools, Kalamazoo County (page 5); Elizabeth O'Dell, St. Joseph County ISD, St. Joseph County (6); Guillermo Z. Lopez, Lansing School District, Ingham County (7); Cory McLaughlin, Jefferson Schools, Monroe County (8); Jack Temsey, Eaton RESA, Eaton County (9); Jason Babbage, Allen Park Public Schools, Wayne County (10); Dr. Anisha Hannah, Pontiac School District, Oakland County (11); Paul Kolin, Bloomfield Hills Schools, Oakland County (12); Roderick Means, Westwood Community School District, Wayne County (13); Randel Meisner, Fitzgerald Public Schools, Macomb County (14); Scott Wallace, Fraser Public Schools (15); Ursula (Wester) Rogers, Romulus Community Schools, Wayne County (16); and Lisa Valerio-Nowc, Clintondale Community Schools, Macomb County (17). The contests named are Region 6 (One-Year Term), Region 7 (Three-Year Term) and Region 8 (Three-Year Term).

**Dr. Anisha Hannah, Pontiac School District, Oakland County (Region 8, three-year term).** She describes education as "the key to unlocking the door of possibilities," argues that too much emphasis has been placed on test scores rather than the whole child, and notes that she is Director of Strategic Partnership & Initiatives with the Pontiac Collective Impact Partnership, leading collaboration among nonprofits, government agencies and educational institutions to improve economic and academic outcomes and supporting Oakland County's goal of 80 by 30. She cites experience as Board President with the City of Pontiac School Board of Education in managing complex budgets and engaging diverse stakeholders, and says she seeks the seat to provide a voice for minority students from lower socioeconomic backgrounds. Her credential block lists 3 years on the board, MASB Certified Boardmember, Award of Merit and Award of Distinction, and offices held as President and Secretary.

**Jason Babbage, Allen Park Public Schools, Wayne County.** An alumnus and lifelong resident of the Allen Park district, he holds a master's degree in automotive systems engineering and a bachelor's degree in mechanical engineering from U-M Dearborn and works at Ford Motor Company as an engineer in exterior automotive lighting, describing himself as one of the top experts in headlamp aim (HLA). He has two children in Allen Park schools, cites his MASB Level 2 award of merit, and identifies unfunded policies, declining enrollment, higher education standards and advances in educational technology as major issues, mentioning sensory rooms and the shift from textbooks to technology. His credential block lists 2 years on the board with the Certified Boardmember Award and Award of Merit.

**Roderick Means, Westwood Community School District, Wayne County.** He centers his vision on equity, innovation and community engagement, and names disparities in educational resources and technology integration as primary concerns. A single parent of two boys, he began as a little league baseball and football coach, served as a Cub and Boy Scout leader from Tiger Cub Coordinator to Cubmaster and assistant Boy Scout leader, and served on high school athletic and booster clubs. For the last 20 years he has worked as an Application Developer at the University of Michigan Ann Arbor. He has served on MASB committees including Government Relations, Bylaws and Policy, and Board Leadership and Training, and as an MASB Board Mentor. His credential block lists 28 years on the board; Certified Boardmember Award, Award of Merit, Award of Distinction, Master Boardmember, Master Diamond, Master Platinum and President's Award; and offices held as President, Vice President, Secretary and Treasurer.

**Paul Kolin, Bloomfield Hills Schools, Oakland County.** He describes education as the cornerstone of society, emphasizes equitable opportunity, removing barriers, supporting educators and innovative practice, and says MASB plays a pivotal role in providing leadership, governance and support to local districts. He references his background in Bloomfield Hills for the last 10 years and prior work as a teacher. His credential block lists 10 years on the board; Certified Boardmember Award, Award of Merit and Award of Distinction; and offices held as President, Vice President, Secretary and Treasurer.

**Randel Meisner, Fitzgerald Public Schools, Macomb County.** His stated concerns are sustainable funding for public education at all levels, teacher retention, teacher shortages, full funding for special education, and offsetting the MPSERS cost. His experience includes the MISD Legislative Committee, MISD Budget Review, annual legislative strategic planning sessions, and attendance at state Annual Leadership Conferences and National School Board Conferences; he has been awarded the MASB President's Award. His credential block lists 12 years on the board; Certified Boardmember Award, Award of Merit, Award of Distinction, Master Boardmember, Master Diamond, Master Platinum and President's Award; and offices held as Vice President, Secretary and Treasurer.

**Scott Wallace, Fraser Public Schools.** He notes that Region 8 includes many students of many different backgrounds, that he and his three children graduated from the district, that he is an Eagle Scout, has coached soccer and basketball, and served four years as an officer on the Board of Directors for the Fraser Soccer Club. He has been President of the Fraser Public Schools Board of Education since 2022 and a board member since 2017, and worked on the MASB legislative committee for three years. His credential block lists 8 years on the board; Certified Boardmember Award, Award of Merit, Award of Distinction and Master Boardmember; and offices held as President, Vice President and Treasurer.

**Lisa Valerio-Nowc, Clintondale Community Schools, Macomb County.** A librarian for over thirty years with school-library and classroom experience, she has been a School Librarian, Library Director of Baker College, and a leader in public libraries, and is currently Assistant Manager/Children's Librarian at the Chaney Branch of the Detroit Public Library. She describes classrooms changing daily with new technology, apps and tools and aims to make her district a safe place to learn and grow. Her credential block lists 2 years on the board, the Certified Boardmember Award and Award of Merit, and Secretary as the office held.

**Ursula (Wester) Rogers, Romulus Community Schools, Wayne County.** She cites disparities in funding, access to resources and growing student mental health needs as the central challenges, particularly for marginalized communities. Her career spans substitute teacher, secretary, human resources professional and school board member, with committee service in policy, human resources, school improvement and curriculum. She has been involved with the Romulus Athletic Club for 24 years as treasurer and cheerleading coach for a youth football organization. Her credential block lists 8 years on the board; Certified Boardmember Award, Award of Merit, Award of Distinction and Master Boardmember; and offices held as President, Secretary and Treasurer.

2025_132_02_21_2025_final_2025_2026_scho.paragraph: Administrative presentation to the Troy School District Board of Education on February 25, 2025 by Assistant Superintendents Christine DiPilato (Secondary Instruction) and Kristine Griffor (Elementary Instruction) recommending the Schools of Choice program parameters for 2025-2026. Using Plante Moran Cresa enrollment projections, the administration recommends accepting applications for 52 Section 105 and 6 Section 105C kindergarten students, 25 Section 105 and 1 Section 105C first graders, and 1 Section 105 plus 1 Section 105c student across grades 6-8. District-wide, 147 elementary Schools of Choice students were enrolled in 2024-2025 against 4862 non-Schools of Choice students, or 2.93%.

**Sibling preference survey**

The district anticipates many more than 8 sibling-preference survey respondents and would admit 58 kindergartners initially, with the option to admit additional students in the third week of August if space allows. Middle school students would be placed in a building according to available space.
2025_132_02_21_2025_final_2025_2026_scho.verbose:
**Presentation and presenters.** "Recommendations for Schools of Choice, 2025-2026 School Year" was delivered to the Troy School District Board of Education on Tuesday, February 25, 2025 by Christine DiPilato, Assistant Superintendent Secondary Instruction, and Kristine Griffor, Assistant Superintendent Elementary Instruction. The opening slide describes the program: Schools of Choice provides non-resident students with additional enrollment opportunities; participation is optional for districts; and the degree and extent of participation - including application enrollment dates, grade levels and building assignment - are determined at the local level.

**Sibling preference survey.** A survey was emailed to current Schools of Choice families requesting information on siblings who would be eligible for kindergarten, first grade and 6th, 7th and 8th grade for the 2025-2026 school year. Responses identified 2 kindergarten students planning to attend under Section 105 and 6 under Section 105c; 0 first grade students under either Section 105 or Section 105c; and for middle school (6th, 7th and 8th combined) 0 under Section 105 and 1 under Section 105c. The note states that the proposal factors in the 9 known SOC siblings above, plus an additional 2 slots giving flexibility to accept any unknown sibling SOC applicants for kindergarten, first grade or 6th to 8th grade.

**Memorandum.** The final slide reproduces a memorandum dated Tuesday, February 25, 2025, to the TSD Board of Education from DiPilato and Griffor on the subject of Schools of Choice recommendations for the 2025-2026 school year. It includes carried-over language from an earlier memo addressing the 2016-2017 school year, which recommended using Fred Ignatovich's 1.5 enrollment projection numbers with his recommended formula (most likely plus low divided by 2), accepting SOC applications for 100 kindergarten and 30 first grade students, limiting SOC kindergarten applicants to the full-day kindergarten program, and accepting sibling preference applications only for siblings of current SOC students to attend Baker Middle School, where enrollment was estimated at approximately 728 and 15 applications would be accepted in the initial process. That older passage also noted that actual February Count enrollment for kindergarten and first grade exceeded both the "Most Likely" and "Low" 2015-16 projections.

**Factors considered and 2025-2026 recommendation.** The factors listed for the 2025-2026 recommendation are current enrollment across the Troy School District; enrollment projections, patterns and trends; numbers and percentages of Schools of Choice students currently in the district; the projected number of SOC siblings who would be age-eligible to enter the district in 2025-2026 if a "Limited" number of kindergarten, first and sixth through eighth grade students were admitted; and available elementary classrooms. After analyzing that data, the administration recommends using Plante Moran Cresa enrollment projection numbers as the foundation for determining how many Schools of Choice students to admit, and accepting SOC applications for Kindergarten of 52 under Section 105 and 6 under Section 105C; First Grade of 25 under Section 105 and 1 under Section 105C; and 6th to 8th grade combined of 1 under Section 105 and 1 under Section 105c. Based on the number of kindergarten applications received for 2024-2025, the administration anticipates attracting many more than 8 sibling preference survey response applicants, which would allow the district to admit 58 kindergartners initially, with the option of admitting additional students in the third week of August if space allows. Middle school students would be placed in a building according to available space.
